title: Type Conversion and static_cast
summary: C++ converts between types automatically when it has to. Some conversions **lose information**. When you want a conversion, say so with `static_cast<Type>(value)`.
markdown:
## Conversions happen without being asked Whenever a value of one type is used where another is expected, C++ converts it. This is called an **implicit conversion**: the compiler does it without you writing anything. ```cpp double d{ 5 }; // the int 5 becomes the double 5.0 int i = 3.9; // the double 3.9 becomes the int 3: the .9 is gone ``` The first is harmless. The second lost information, and nothing warned you. ## Widening and narrowing ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph SAFE["Widening: always fits"] direction LR c["char"] --> s["short"] --> i["int"] --> l["long long"] f["float"] --> d["double"] end subgraph RISKY["Narrowing: may lose information"] direction LR d2["double 3.9"] --> i2["int 3"] l2["long long
5 billion"] --> i3["int
does not fit"] end ``` | | Direction | Safe? | |---|---|---| | **Widening** | To a type that can hold every value of the original | Yes | | **Narrowing** | To a type that cannot | Only if you know the value fits | This is why the course uses braces. Brace initialization **refuses** to narrow: ```cpp int a = 3.5; // compiles; a is 3 int b{ 3.5 }; // error: narrowing conversion ``` ## Mixed arithmetic When an operator has two different types to work with, the compiler converts one side first so both match. Roughly, the "smaller" type is converted to the "larger" one. | Expression | Result type | Note | |---|---|---| | `int + double` | `double` | | | `int + long long` | `long long` | | | `char + char` | `int` | types smaller than `int` are widened to `int` first | | `int + unsigned` | `unsigned` | the trap from [[2.02 Integers]] | The important detail: the conversion happens **one operator at a time**, not for the statement as a whole. ```cpp #include int main() { int total{ 7 }; int count{ 2 }; double wrong{ static_cast(total / count) }; // 3 double right{ static_cast(total) / count }; // 3.5 std::cout << wrong << ' ' << right << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ```mermaid flowchart TD A["total / count"] --> B["int / int gives 3"] --> C["converted afterwards: 3.0
the .5 is already lost"] D["static_cast<double>(total) / count"] --> E["double / int
count is widened to double"] --> F["3.5"] ``` In the first line the division is finished, as integer division, before any `double` is involved. ## Converting on purpose `static_cast` is how you tell the compiler, and the next reader, "I mean this conversion". ```cpp static_cast(value) ``` ```cpp double price{ 9.99 }; int whole{ static_cast(price) }; // 9 char letter{ static_cast(72) }; // 'H' int code{ static_cast('H') }; // 72 ``` It also satisfies brace initialization, because you have stated your intent: ```cpp int b{ static_cast(3.5) }; // fine: 3 ``` > [!tip] Why not the shorter `(int)price`? > That older form comes from C and still compiles. It will attempt almost any conversion, including dangerous ones, and it is hard to search for. `static_cast` only performs sensible conversions and stands out in the code. ## Converting is not rounding `static_cast` **cuts off** the decimals. It does not round. For rounding, use ``. | Call | Result | Rule | |---|---|---| | `static_cast(2.9)` | `2` | cut off | | `std::round(2.5)` | `3.0` | to the nearest whole number | | `std::floor(2.9)` | `2.0` | always down | | `std::ceil(2.1)` | `3.0` | always up | The `` functions return a `double`. To store a rounded value in an `int`, combine the two: ```cpp int rounded{ static_cast(std::round(2.7)) }; // 3 ``` ## Other casts exist C++ has three more named casts for specialised jobs. You will not need them for a long time. The one you will meet is `dynamic_cast`, in [[8.06 Object Slicing, Casting and Composition]]. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does `double x{ 5 / 2 };` hold? - `2.5` + `2.0` - `3.0` - Nothing; it does not compile > `5 / 2` is integer division, giving 2, and only then is it converted to `double`. Write `5.0 / 2` to get 2.5. ? What is the type of `'a' + 'b'`? - `char` - `std::string` + `int` - `bool` > Types smaller than `int` are widened to `int` before arithmetic, so adding two `char`s gives an `int`, not a joined string. ? Does `static_cast(3.99)` round? + No, it cuts off the decimals and gives `3` - Yes, it gives `4` - Yes, it rounds to the nearest even number - No, it keeps `3.99` and only changes the label > Converting a decimal to an integer type drops everything after the point. Use `std::round` first if you want rounding. ? What is a narrowing conversion? - A conversion that makes a value smaller, such as from 10 to 5 - Any conversion written with `static_cast` + A conversion to a type that cannot hold every value of the original, so information may be lost - A conversion from a wide character to a normal one > Narrowing goes to a type with a smaller range or less precision, such as `double` to `int`. Brace initialization refuses it. ```
ideas:
1. Read two `int` values and print their average correctly as a `double`.
2. Print `static_cast<int>(-2.7)` and `std::round(-2.7)`. Why do they differ?
3. Print `'a' + 1` and `static_cast<char>('a' + 1)`. Explain the two results.

cards.a:
`2.0`

`5 / 2` is integer division, giving 2, and only then is it converted to `double`. Write `5.0 / 2` to get 2.5.

`int`

Types smaller than `int` are widened to `int` before arithmetic, so adding two `char`s gives an `int`, not a joined string.

No, it cuts off the decimals and gives `3`

Converting a decimal to an integer type drops everything after the point. Use `std::round` first if you want rounding.

A conversion to a type that cannot hold every value of the original, so information may be lost

Narrowing goes to a type with a smaller range or less precision, such as `double` to `int`. Brace initialization refuses it.
